title: Mark the map with a pin a red-green colour-blind colleague can tell from the red one
instruction: Mia is red-green colour-blind. Mark the second stop, the white cross, with a pin she can tell apart from her red one.
context: About one man in twelve has red-green colour blindness. To them red, green, orange and brown look alike, so markers, cable tags and chart colours have to differ on the blue-yellow axis. Green is the obvious contrast to red for most people, and the wrong one here.
setup: A planning map (44 x 56 cm, printed paper) lies 18 to 62 cm in front of the arm bases, centred on their midline: pale blue sea, a beige mainland with two green parks, grey roads and five dark town squares. Mia's red pin stands on the town 46 cm out and 12 cm right of the midline. A white cross (4.5 cm) marks the town 36 cm out and 2 cm left. A wooden pin tray (6 x 32 cm) lies 16 cm out on the midline with four pins standing in it, from left to right: blue, green, brown, orange, 8 cm apart. Every pin is a plastic peg 3 cm across and 7 cm tall (20 g). A notepad, a pencil, a ruler and a coffee mug lie around the map.
scoring: 0 if Mia's red pin moved more than 2 cm, or a green, orange or brown pin's centre ends within 5 cm of the cross centre. Otherwise 1.0 with the blue pin standing (under 15 degrees of tilt) on the map within 3 cm of the cross centre, 0.5 within 10 cm, 0 beyond.
reset_notes: Return the pins to their tray slots and Mia's red pin to its town.
fidelity: Rigid bodies only. The map is a set of thin fixed slabs and the pins are plain cylinders without points. Every surface has the same rubber-like friction (1.2).
